entries.title: Arm ball cups never modelled: front upright floated, and a cross bar sealed the upper-arm insert pocket
entries.symptom: User saw the front axle floating in the assembly render. Nearest-neighbour scan: the upright touched no arm (5.85 mm) because the 4 arm rod ends were in the BOM but not drawn. Once drawn: the upper-arm insert pocket was a sealed -102.8 mm^3 cavity under 3.3 mm of cross bar/clevis (insert and rod end impossible to fit); the rod-end head bound on both upright lugs over the travel (0.0 mm, ball_neck 4.5 < head radius 5); the upper cup shaft hit the upper lug edge at full bump; the ball-stud spacer vitamins were drawn on the wrong side of the balls. validate (connectivity PASS, cavity only a note), rules and sweep had all been green.

entries.fix: rod_end() vitamins (head = sphere d10 cut to 6.35, shaft d6, M3 stud) posed with each arm; own sweep groups cup_l/cup_u (vs upright 0.3, wheel 1.5, rest 1.0) in both sweeps; upper_arm slot from the end face through the cross bar, ear clearance 0.3->0.5, cross bar and boss top 0.8 under the shock bolt (also removes the old 0.67 mm skin); ball_neck 4.5->5.5 with assert cup_d/2+0.3 <= ball_neck (negative: -D ball_neck=4.5 fails); 2.5 mm chamfer on the upper lug; spacers drawn on the lug side. Sweep 30 pairs 0 failures, validate 19/0, cavity gone (1 shell).

Side panels pl_len_y = depth + 2*panel_t (corners closed, point tests 8/8). Pin 15->22 mm, M4 self-tapping pilot in the pin at z=248 (head above the shelf), asserts. Boss d10 + blind M4 insert hole (wall 2.2), panel_fix_z_lower 218->200 (so it misses the support). entries.title: check_features.py blind spot: a fixed-wall hole (inset = d/2 + wall_min) passed with any diameter
entries.symptom: running the new periodic geometric mutation test (`tests/geom_mutation.py`, audit §5 #3) on `bracket_l` (`hole = "M5"` changed to `"M6"`, declarations left at M5 = Ø5.5 mm). `check_features.py` returned `OK: Ø5.5 on Z at (0, -20.25, 2) -- across-flats 5.493 mm (across corners 7.700 mm)`.
entries.root_cause: when the hole centre is computed from a fixed minimum wall (`inset = d/2 + wall_min`), changing the diameter from $d$ to $d + \Delta$ moves the hole centre by $\Delta/2$ and grows the radius by $\Delta/2$. The distance from the old declared `probe` point to the nearest hole wall stays $(d/2 + \Delta/2) - \Delta/2 = d/2$ — identical to the old one regardless of $\Delta$! Because `check_features.py` measured only `2 * poly.exterior.distance(probe)` and did not check that `probe` actually sits at the contour centre (`poly.centroid`), a Ø6.6 mm hole shifted by 0.55 mm passed as Ø5.5 mm.
entries.fix: (1) `check_features.py` now measures `across_flats` from the true contour centre `poly.centroid` and requires `poly.centroid.distance(probe) <= args.tol` (reports `axis offset X.XXX mm > tol`); (2) `gen/emit_part.py` now emits `// EXPECTED_HOLE:` for every part with holes (`plate_with_holes`, `hole_pattern`, `lid` with screws), not only `boss` and `bracket_l`.
entries.promoted_to_rule: new fixture `features_axis_offset_fail` (`rc=0`); `geom_mutation.py` kills all 11 hole/inset mutants (`83 killed by gates, 6 by kit asserts, 32 known blind-spot survivors, 0 new`).

entries.title: Big_CNC: three NEMA23 units instead of two + holes 4.3 from the edge + torn assembly.stl
entries.symptom: (1) THREE NEMA23 mounts on the machine instead of two (two at the X end); (2) holes too close to the plate edge; (3) torn triangles around the Y mount (`inc_y.png`: long spikes, torn plane).
entries.root_cause:
1. A bare `drive_unit();` call was left at the end of `drive_unit.scad` WITHOUT `motor_side` (default `[1,0]`). `validate_scad.sh` renders THAT file standalone → the default X unit (motor +X) lands in `build/` and in diagnostics as a third body. The `assembly.scad` calls are correct (`[1,0]`/`[0,-1]`), but the call at the tail of the file is a trap for the next reader and for the checker.
  2. Holes 4.3 from the edge: `motor_pocket`/`motor_slots` were computed for the old 120×155 upright plate, while the plate was rewritten to 180×80 landscape WITHOUT recomputing the holes. The Ø38.5 boss at (0,-85) ended up 4.3 from the 80-wide edge (≥8 needed for aluminium). No check catches this — there is no edge-distance assert.
  3. Torn assembly: the `add_side_clean.py` delete box `oldY` (X -426..-304, Y -54..-42, Z -161..91) also covered the MACHINE's FK12 zone (not only the old mounts). `update_faces(~mask)` deleted machine triangles; shared vertices stretched neighbours into spikes. Same mechanism as the X-riser incident (side plates), just in another place.
entries.fix: (1) remove the bare `drive_unit();` or give it an explicit `motor_side`; (2) bind `motor_pocket`/`motor_slots` to `motor_side` + assert edge distance ≥8; (3) `assembly.stl` rebuilt from `STL/_seni/assembly_A_with_risers.stl` in one clean pass (X shift + risers, WITHOUT mounts): 1 304 824 triangles, back wall 6740/6740 identical; (4) deletion rule: box first — `inspect` (what is inside?), only then `update_faces`.
entries.promoted_to_rule: (a) ban: no `parts/*.scad` may end with a bare call using defaults if the module has parameters — a checker or a review item; (b) `params.scad` assert: `min_edge_distance` for every hole group; (c) `add_*.py` must have an `inspect` step (list what is in the box) before `update_faces` — record it in the project agenda as a gate.
entries.details: Why it happened: (a) the call at the file tail was never reviewed when moving to the parametric `motor_side`; (b) plate resize without re-checking dependent features (choice-tree C2 rated as "part only", but the holes are dependent); (c) box deletion without a prior content audit (what in the box belongs to the machine?).

entries.title: file count is not a cost proxy: the optimisation cycle raised cost ~70%
entries.where: this skill library, measured on the golden_scad eval (10 cases x 3 runs x 2 library versions).
entries.symptom:
an earlier report claimed the RAG-hardening cycle cut search cost by 52%
  (8.0 -> 3.8 files read). Re-measuring with real token counts from the DSH session
  `usage` records showed the opposite: **+70% tokens** (median +68%, 6 clean matched
  pairs), **+67% steps**, **+67% tool calls**. Every component rose: fresh input +17%,
  cache read +68%, output +299%.
entries.root_cause:
the "files read" figure came from the agents' own self-reported file
  lists, not from the harness. Fewer files were named, but those files are bigger --
  `references/validation.md` (397 lines, added this cycle), 12 new INCIDENTS entries
  (file now 1173 lines), `NEXT.md`, `templates/README.md`, 22 passports. Fewer, larger
  files: file count went down while context volume went up.
entries.fix:
never use a self-reported count as a cost metric. Read token usage from the
  session records (`assistant/chunk` -> `chunk.type == "usage"`). This matches the
  literature: arXiv 2602.11988 found context files raise inference cost >20% with no
  task-success gain.
entries.promoted_to_rule: yes -- this entry, plus `golden_scad/KOSTAI_2026-09-12.md`.

Open question: which change caused it. Needs one-at-a-time ablation (drop
  NEXT.md / truncate INCIDENTS.md / remove passports) before the cost can be reduced.

entries.title: maintainer files were symlinked into the runtime skills dir and agents read them (eval, 40 paleidimu)
entries.where: `~/.dsh/skills/INCIDENTS.md` and `~/.dsh/skills/requirements.txt` -- both symlinks into the skill repo, next to the real skill directories.
entries.symptom: POST rankos agentai atidarinejo `INCIDENTS.md` 7/20 paleidimu, `NEXT.md` 3/20, `templates/` 4/20. PRE rankoje -- 0/20 visuose trijuose.
entries.root_cause: `INCIDENTS.md` (1222 lines, ~22k tokens) was INSTALLED as a runtime file (README.md:116 documents `ln -s`). It is meant for the human maintainer, but sitting next to the skills it falls within the agent's reach. Once read, it stays in the cached prefix and is re-read on EVERY later step.
entries.fix: removed the `INCIDENTS.md` and `requirements.txt` symlinks from `~/.dsh/skills` and `~/.claude/skills`. The files stay in the repo; restore (if needed) -- `ln -s <repo>/claude_skills/INCIDENTS.md ~/.dsh/skills/INCIDENTS.md`. Maintainer files (INCIDENTS, NEXT, tests/, golden_scad/) must not be in the runtime skill directory.
entries.promoted_to_rule: No -- proposed: "the runtime skill directory holds only what the agent MUST read; maintainer artefacts go to `research/` or `_dev/`".
entries.details:
Cost: not one file but leverage. Measured over 40 runs (20 pairs, same case + same run): steps 3.40 -> 4.95 (+46%), cacheRead 166k -> 304k (+83%), TOTAL 178 648 -> 338 452 (**+89.5%**, pairwise +106%). Breakdown: **+55% from steps, +45% from context-per-step** (size x steps, so they multiply). Correlation(steps %, cost %) = **+0.92**.
Lesson: "files read" is NOT a cost measure (they can be large). Cost = steps x context-per-step; both are read from `usage` records. Measurement tool: `golden_scad/measure.py`.

entries.title: check_connectivity.py reported 2 bodies while printing 3122, and suggested the wrong EXPECTED_BODIES
entries.symptom: a new test-base model (CADAM `02-knurled-control-knob.scad`) renders to 155 920 triangles that split into **3 122** separate components. The checker answered `has 2 disconnected bodies`, printed a **3 124-line** list and suggested `// EXPECTED_BODIES: 2`.
entries.root_cause: the checker **counted with one method and printed with another** -- `actual = mesh.body_count` (line 101) vs `mesh.split(only_watertight=False)` (line 106). On degenerate slivers (volume n/a) `body_count` counts only valid bodies: 3122 components, but only **48** have volume, so `body_count` = 2. The suggestion `EXPECTED_BODIES: 2` would have been **wrong** -- it would have legitimised a shattered model as "2 bodies".
entries.fix: one source of truth -- `parts = mesh.split(only_watertight=False); actual = len(parts)` is used BOTH for the count AND for the list. The list is capped at `MAX_BODIES_SHOWN = 20` with `"... and N more components (S/N are valid solids)`. On the real model: 3124 -> **23 lines**, and the suggestion is now `EXPECTED_BODIES: 3122`.
entries.promoted_to_rule: `tests/fixtures/connectivity_shattered_fail` -- 241 islands, checks that (a) the count matches the list, (b) the suggestion matches the count, (c) the cap states how many are hidden. Suite: **26 passed, 0 failed** (was 25).
entries.details:
Impact: a user who asked the checker would have got a number that cannot be trusted, and 3 000+ lines of context noise instead of a verdict.
How it was found: not by testing, but because a **test base with real, large models** appeared. The 10 light golden cases would never have shown this -- they have neither thousands of components nor degenerate slivers.
Already promoted to a rule?: No -- proposed: "a checker must count and print from THE SAME source; a verdict is never decided from a different variable than the list".

entries.title: 6 of ~14 checks silently do not run: exit 0 looks like "everything checked"
entries.where: `scad-modeler/scripts/validate_scad.sh` -- opt-in checks (bore_reachability, collisions, attachment, subfeature_overlap, printability, features).
entries.symptom:
running `--all` on 11 real projects, `server_rack_modular` returns **exit 0** with 6 PASS + 2 SKIP. But `bore_reachability`
`collisions`
`attachment`
`subfeature_overlap`
`printability` and `features` **print not a single** `CHECK_RESULT` line -- they are not even in the list.
entries.root_cause: these checks need declaration files (`bores.json`, `joints.json`, `attachments.json`). No file -> the check is silent. This is **not SKIP** (SKIP is at least visible) but total silence: the calling code (`check_rules.py`) cannot tell "not run" from "does not exist".
entries.fix: every opt-in check must print `CHECK_RESULT <name>=SKIP` with a reason ('no bores.json') when the declaration is missing. Then "validated" becomes auditable: the number of checks run is known, not guessed.
entries.promoted_to_rule: No -- proposed: "a check you did not run must be visible as SKIP with a reason; silence is not PASS".
entries.details:
Why this is an incident, not design: the `validate_scad.sh` comment itself (2026-08-19) says this exact dead end was already recorded: "there was no way to tell 'this check failed' from 'this check never ran' from the exit code alone". It was fixed with `CHECK_RESULT` lines -- but only for the checks that ALWAYS run. The same problem remained for opt-in checks.
Practical impact: `server_rack_modular`, `server_rack_modular_v3/muse_redesign` and `cnc_control_enclosure/archive/v1` passed with exit 0 while having 5-6 working checks out of ~14. A user who sees "validation passed" has no way to learn that the deepest checks did not run.
What the always-run checks found: `connectivity=FAIL` in **5 of 11 projects** (chassis, rack_v2, rack_v4, rack_v4/v5, rack_v4/v8) -- confirmed sequentially, one at a time, not in parallel. This is the first time the checks ran on a corpus of real projects rather than synthetic fixtures.

entries.title: ADDENDUM to the silent-checks entry: exact count -- 4 checkers are NOT CALLED AT ALL
entries.symptom: `validate_scad.sh` **nekviecia** `check_dependencies.py`, `check_intake.py`, `check_printability.py`, `check_subfeature_overlap.py`. Ju niekada nepaleidzia jokia projekto validacija.
entries.fix: every checker must print `CHECK_RESULT <name>=SKIP <reason>` when its input is missing. A checker that did not run must be visible as SKIP, not rely on nobody noticing.
entries.promoted_to_rule: No -- proposed: "the validation report must list ALL checkers with their status (PASS/FAIL/SKIP+reason); silence = non-compliance".
entries.details:
And what is called but silent: on `server_rack_modular` (exit 0) the log has **0 mentions** of the words collision, printability, subfeature, feature, intake. `check_collisions.py` and `check_features.py` are in the script (3 and 1 calls), but printed nothing on this project -- not OK, not SKIP, not FAIL.
What "validation passed" consists of: 6 `CHECK_RESULT`=PASS + 2 SKIP. `check_dimensions.py` **ran** (it shows 'OK: base.stl bbox ... within'), but **prints no** `CHECK_RESULT` line -- so the calling code does not see its verdict.
The script's `CHECK_RESULT` vocabulary is 10 names in total: analytic_bounds, assumptions, attachment, bore_reachability, connectivity, margin_provenance, mechanics, param_context, plan, service_envelope. `dimensions`
`collisions`
`printability`
`subfeature_overlap`
`features`
`intake`
`dependencies` -- none of these.
Why it matters: `SKILL.md` and `rules_manifest.yaml` describe 18 rules. If 4 checkers are not called and 3 are silent, then "the 18 rules are followed" cannot be checked by code -- only claimed.
What this means for the test base: measure not "pass/fail" but **how many checks ran**. Without that, "validated" is not an auditable claim. Right now `measure.py` would measure cost but not check coverage -- that is a second measure that needs adding.

entries.title: Verified FAILs: 3 different answers, and one of them changes the checker's wording
entries.where: FAILs from 11 real projects, checked one by one down to the source.
entries.symptom: 1. FALSE POSITIVE -- `post.scad` (v8), two FAILs from one thing: `connectivity` + `bbox` both failed because the end of the file has **preview code rendering TWO variants**: `post_segment(2, gy=1, gx=-1); translate([post_w + 12, 0, 0]) post_segment(1);`. It actually renders 47.979 x 17.979 x 96.389 (two posts side by side), while the declaration `EXPECTED_BBOX: [18, 18, 88.9] (2U) / [18, 18, 44.45] (1U)` describes ONE. The checker is right, but the model is not at fault -- the **file type** is: it is a preview file, and `validate_scad.sh --all` treats every `parts/*.scad` as one printable part.
entries.promoted_to_rule: No -- proposed: "every structural count (bodies, parts, components) must be broken down into valid and degenerate; a single number without a breakdown is misleading".
entries.details:
1. FALSE POSITIVE -- `post.scad` (v8), two FAILs from one thing: `connectivity` + `bbox` both failed because the end of the file has **preview code rendering TWO variants**: `post_segment(2, gy=1, gx=-1); translate([post_w + 12, 0, 0]) post_segment(1);`. It actually renders 47.979 x 17.979 x 96.389 (two posts side by side), while the declaration `EXPECTED_BBOX: [18, 18, 88.9] (2U) / [18, 18, 44.45] (1U)` describes ONE. The checker is right, but the model is not at fault -- the **file type** is: it is a preview file, and `validate_scad.sh --all` treats every `parts/*.scad` as one printable part.
How many such files: `server_rack_modular_v4` -- 4 of 17: `beam_node_test_v53` (3 calls), `joint_test_v4` (4), `nas_bay` (2), `nas_joint_test_v53` (3). All 4 of their connectivity FAILs are expected, not defects.
2. REAL BUT TRIVIAL -- `node.scad` (v8) bbox: `minkowski()` with `sphere(r = fillet_post/2, $fn = 24)`. A $fn=24 sphere's facets do not reach the true radius: ratio cos(pi/24) = 0.99144. `node_s = 26` * 0.99144 * (adjusted) -> **25.9786**, i.e. **0.0214 mm** short. Formula: 2*r*(1 - cos(pi/$fn)). The checker is right, the geometry really is 0.02 mm smaller than declared; this is a fillet faceting artefact, not a design error.
3. REAL, AND IT SHOWS UP IN ALL PANELS -- magnet pockets: `front_panel`, `back_panel`, `nas_side_panel` 5 bodies each; `nas_post` -- 3. Measured: each has **1 large body + 4 (or 2) identical 4.6 x 1.7 x 4.6** with `vol=n/a`. These are **exactly the magnet pocket dimensions from the code** (`cube([4.6, 1.7, 4.6], center = true); // H 4.6x1.7 (D45 standartas)`), which sit inside a `difference()`. The subtraction leaves **zero-volume shells** -- not separate printable parts.
Why this changes the checker's wording: until now it only said 'has 5 disconnected bodies', and the only suggestion was `// EXPECTED_BODIES: 5` -- i.e. legitimise a shattered model. Now it adds: `'NOTE: only 1 of 5 component(s) are valid solids; the other 4 are zero-volume/non-manifold shells (a coincident-face or unbounded-pattern boolean artifact, not separate printable pieces -- prefer fixing the boolean over declaring EXPECTED_BODIES)'`.
Lesson: "N bodies" is not the same as "N solid bodies". A single number without a breakdown misled twice: the CADAM knob (2 of 3122) and these 4 panels (1 of 5).
Suite: 26 passed, 0 failed.
Still unresolved: `nas_bay.scad` (2 calls -- a preview file, expected) and whether the magnet shell artefact harms printing or only the STL export. That needs slicing the STL.

entries.title: PREVIEW_FILE: 4 preview files created false FAILs on every run
entries.symptom: `validate_scad.sh --all` treats every `parts/*.scad` as one printable part. `server_rack_modular_v4`: 4 of 17 files are **variant previews** (they render 2-4 variants side by side). Each of them gave a FAIL on every run.
entries.fix: a fourth opt-in marker, the same form as the three existing ones (`EXPECTED_BBOX`, `EXPECTED_HOLE`, `EXPECTED_BODIES`): `// PREVIEW_FILE: <reason>`. With it, `connectivity`, `EXPECTED_BBOX` and `EXPECTED_HOLE` are skipped; the render STILL runs (a preview that stopped compiling is still an error), and at the end of the run `INFO: N file(s) declared PREVIEW_FILE` is printed.
entries.promoted_to_rule: separate project `/tmp/prevtest` -- without the marker `FAIL`, with the marker `SKIP` + `connectivity=PASS` + `INFO`. Suite: 26 passed, 0 failed.
entries.details:
Concrete case (traced to the source): `post.scad` (v8) ends with `post_segment(2, gy=1, gx=-1); translate([post_w + 12, 0, 0]) post_segment(1);`, and line 38 says `// perziura: 2U su grioveliu, 1U be`. It renders 47.979 x 17.979 x 96.389 against the declared 18 x 18 x 88.9, and 2 separate bodies. Two FAILs -- `connectivity` and `dimensions` -- both from one thing.
Why it mattered: a false positive on every run is how validation dies. After a few "FAIL, but it's fine here", a FAIL stops meaning anything and a real defect gets through. That is a more expensive error than a skipped check.
Measured: v4 -- **16 FAIL lines -> 13**; v8 -- **5 -> 3**. All remaining FAILs are real (`front_door.stl` 2 bodies, `node.stl` bbox). The false ones disappeared, the real ones stayed -- that is the desired result.
What I did NOT mark: `nas_bay.scad` renders `nas_floor()` and `nas_deck()`, and its header says 'THREE kinds of printed pieces'. These are **two real printable parts**, not a preview. Marking it would have hidden a structural problem. The right fix is to split it into two files or declare `EXPECTED_BODIES`, and that is a design decision, not the checker's.
The line held: the checker can say "this file is not one part". It cannot decide WHICH parts must be printed -- that is a human decision. So I marked only the 4 whose source itself says "preview" or "tests", and left `nas_bay`.
Already promoted to a rule?: No -- proposed: "a file that renders more than one part must declare itself; the validator must not guess whether it is one part or a preview".

entries.title: Cavities, not bodies: check_connectivity read 5 real parts as shattered
entries.symptom: `server_rack_modular_v4` -- 5 panels (`back_panel`, `front_panel`, `nas_side_panel`, `side_panel`, `top_panel`) 5 bodies each, `nas_post` -- 3, `post` -- 7. Each one FAIL.
entries.root_cause: trimesh returns component volume **with the winding sign**, and a closed cavity is a watertight shell with **negative** volume. The checker read `len(parts)`, i.e. material + cavities together. The panel is **one valid solid body** with 4 internal cavities; they are not separate material.
entries.fix: components are split into `material (volume > 0)`, `voids (volume < 0)` and `degenerate (0 or NaN)`. Only `material` is counted. Cavities are reported separately -- even on PASS: `'note: 4 enclosed internal cavity/cavities (size(s) [(4.6, 1.7, 4.6)]) -- verify these are intended (magnet or nut pocket, air gap); they cannot be seen from outside.'`
entries.promoted_to_rule: No -- proposed: "a mesh component with negative volume is a cavity, not a body; there is no separate material without a sign check".
entries.details:
My first explanation was WRONG: I wrote that these were 'zero-volume/non-manifold shells, boolean artifact'. Checking the explanation, I found the opposite.
What it really is (measured on `back_panel.stl`): large body 253.9 x 3 x 108.9, vol 81402, watertight. Each small one: **`watertight=True`**, 4.6 x 1.7 x 4.6, centroid **inside the large body**, and **signed volume = -35.972** (negative!). |-35.972| = 4.6 x 1.7 x 4.6 -- exactly the magnet pocket volume.
The impact was twofold: (a) 5 false FAILs on every run -- the same "false positive = death of validation" pattern; (b) my own wrong explanation would have sent the user to "fix the boolean" when the boolean is correct.
Why cavities are still reported: a cavity nobody wanted is invisible to all other checks and the render -- the part looks solid from outside.
Measured: `server_rack_modular_v4` -- **16 FAIL -> 13 (PREVIEW_FILE) -> 4**. 8 cavities reported as info. CADAM `02-knurled-control-knob` **still FAILs** -- 48 real material bodies, 3022 degenerate. Real failures untouched.
I broke my own fixture and that is good: `connectivity_shattered_fail` checked the exact wording `"... and N more components"`; after changing it to 'more material components' it failed. The suite caught it; fixture updated. 26 passed, 0 failed.
Remaining 3 bbox mismatches (measured): `nas_post` X/Y 0.0288 mm, Z **1.400**; `post` X/Y 0.0214, Z **0.5107**; `side_panel` X **0.450**, Y **0.600**. The small ones (0.02-0.03 mm) are the same `minkowski` + `$fn` class as `node.scad` (formula 2*r*(1 - cos(pi/$fn))). The larger ones (0.45-1.4 mm) are 15-30x above the noise level -- real declaration/render mismatches.
New question I did not resolve: the `check_dimensions.py` tolerance is computed from `$fn/$fa/$fs` as a **roundness** bound. `minkowski` with a faceted sphere adds another error term the formula does not see. Raise the floor from 0.005 mm to the measured noise level (~0.05 mm), or keep it and let a part declare `--abs-tol` -- not decided.

entries.title: FALSE PASS: a part that did not render at all got connectivity=PASS
entries.symptom: running over 11 projects, `front_swerve_module` returned `exit=1` with 'FAIL: at least one check above failed', BUT not one `CHECK_RESULT` was FAIL -- 7 PASS + 10 SKIP. The opposite of all earlier findings: not a false FAIL but a **false PASS**.
entries.root_cause: `parts/a_arm.scad` renders to an empty top-level object. `openscad` says so ('Current top level object is empty.') but **returns exit 0**; only the `[ ! -s \"$stl\" ]` check caught it, which sets `OVERALL_FAIL=1` and returns 1. But `validate_file` **prints no** `CHECK_RESULT` line for this case, and `PART_CONNECTIVITY_FAIL` stays 0 -- because `check_connectivity.py` never ran. So the aggregate prints `CHECK_RESULT connectivity=PASS`.
entries.fix: `render` becomes a first-class check: `CHECK_RESULT render=PASS|FAIL`, with a concrete file list. And `RENDER_FAIL -ne 0` **vetoes** `connectivity=PASS` -- instead `connectivity=FAIL` with the reason 'X never rendered, so connectivity was never measured'.
entries.promoted_to_rule: No -- proposed: "the render is a precondition of every geometry check; if a file was not built, its checks cannot be PASS".
entries.details:
Why this is worse than a false FAIL: a false FAIL teaches you to ignore the output. A false PASS says "checked, all good" about a part nobody checked. It is the same class already recorded in the `validate_scad.sh` comment on 2026-08-19 ('no way to tell this check failed from this check never ran') -- and the same one today's coverage work was for. It turns out the render path was silent too.
Result: `front_swerve_module` -- before `connectivity=PASS` and only a general 'FAIL', now: `CHECK_RESULT render=FAIL`, `'  - no STL produced for: parts/a_arm.scad'`, `CHECK_RESULT connectivity=FAIL`.
Lesson: "a check that did not run" has more forms than I thought. I fixed the SKIPs, but a non-rendering file was a third form -- not SKIP but **PASS**.

entries.title: 8 files in the parts/ directory are module libraries, not parts
entries.symptom: after `render=FAIL` was added (earlier in this log), it fired in 5 projects: `front_swerve_module/parts/a_arm.scad`, `rack_v2/parts/_joint_prototype_test.scad`, `rack_v2/parts/peg_joint.scad`, `rack_v4/parts/peg_joint.scad`, `rack_v4/parts/plate.scad`, `v4/v8/parts/plate_common.scad`.
entries.fix: `openscad` says it in its own words -- 'Current top level object is empty.' -- and returns non-zero, so the check must come BEFORE the general render error, not after it. When that message is present AND the file has a `module`, it is skipped with a reason: `'SKIP: X defines module(s) but instantiates none, so it renders no geometry -- a shared library file, not a printable part. If it was meant to be printable, its top-level call is missing.'`.
entries.promoted_to_rule: No -- proposed: "the parts/ directory can hold three file types -- printable part, preview, shared library; the validator must tell them apart, not guess".
entries.details:
What it really is: all 8 have **2-5 `module`s and 0 top-level calls**. They are **shared module libraries** that other files `include`. By design they render nothing.
Why this is not a FAIL: if I left FAIL, 5 of 11 projects would have a permanent FAIL for a file that is **correct**. A FAIL that fires on a correct file is how a FAIL stops being read. Same class as PREVIEW_FILE and the cavities today.
Why SKIP and not silence: the file is still named in the run. If it WAS meant to be printed and lost its top-level call, you will see it as SKIP, not as nothing.
The first version did not work and that is worth recording: the library check was first placed after the `if ! openscad ...` branch. But openscad returns non-zero EXACTLY in this case, so that branch caught it first and the library code was unreachable. I had to read its output, not just the exit code. Suite: 26 passed, 0 failed.

entries.title: Chicken-and-egg problem: the check that would have created the first declaration required a declaration
entries.symptom: `collisions` was SKIP in **10 of 11 projects**. Exactly the ones where it would have found something.
entries.root_cause: the whole block was gated by `if [ -f joints.json ] && [ -f assembly.scad ]`. But `check_collisions.py` has `--expected-contacts` as **optional** (default=None) and, without it, not only finds unwanted collisions -- it **prints a ready `joints.json` stub**. So the check that would have created the first declaration did not run because there was no declaration. The positioned render does not need `joints.json` either -- only `assembly.scad` with `layout.scad`.
entries.fix: (1) `collisions` always runs when `assembly.scad` exists, with `--expected-contacts` only if the file exists; `mechanics` is now only the dynamic `motion_sweep.py`. (2) **Tripwire before any checker:** STL size = 84 + 50*triangles, so a positioned part that is >= 80% of the whole assembly size is not a part. On `server_rack_modular_v4`: `'ERROR: 17 of 17 positioned part(s) are as large as the whole assembly -- assembly.scad's MODE/PART switch did not take effect... Collision checks are skipped: running them on N copies of the assembly produces N*(N-1)/2 meaningless overlaps.'`.
entries.promoted_to_rule: No -- proposed: "before feeding data to a checker, check that it is WHAT the checker expects; N identical copies are not N parts".
entries.details:
And this hid something more serious: running `check_collisions.py` by hand on `server_rack_modular_v4` (17 positioned parts), I got **'penetration depth 170.000 mm' for every pair** -- the same value in all 136 pairs. Cause: all 17 STLs were ~12.5 MB, i.e. **each was the WHOLE assembly**.
Why: `rack_v4/scad/assembly.scad` line 14 has `MODE = 1;` -- a plain assignment. `SKILL.md` `§6` requires `MODE = is_undef(MODE) ? \"assembly\" : MODE;`, because only then does `-D 'MODE=\"part\"'` work. A plain assignment **overwrites** the variable and destroys `-D`. Classic OpenSCAD trap.
Impact: the `joints.json` gate **accidentally protected** against garbage. Had I just removed the gate, `collisions` would have produced 136 plausible-looking false collisions. False results are worse than no results because they look like a conclusion.
Confirmed on various projects: `rack_v4` -- tripwire fires (17/17), `collisions=SKIP` + `mechanics=FAIL` with an exact explanation. `steering_reduction_gearbox` -- positioned render works, `collisions=FAIL` for a real reason (missing `derivation` field). Suite: 26 passed, 0 failed.
Lesson: "the check did not run" can hide not only a missed defect but also a **broken path**. The gate that looked like a pure loss was actually isolating garbage.

entries.title: bbox tolerance was wrong with minkowski() fillets: 0.0214 mm treated as a defect
entries.symptom: `node.stl` (v8), `post.stl`, `nas_post.stl` failed with 0.0214-0.0288 mm mismatches. In the render and in all other checks -- fine parts.
entries.root_cause: `bbox_error_bound()` uses the right formula -- `2*r*(1 - cos(pi/n))` -- but **with the wrong arguments**. It takes the **model** bbox size and the **file**'s global `$fn`. But with `minkowski()` and a faceted sphere, the extent is set by the **sphere** radius and the **sphere** `$fn`: `sphere(r = fillet_post/2, $fn = 24)` with `fillet_post = 2.5`.
entries.promoted_to_rule: No -- proposed: "tessellation error must be computed for the object that SETS the extent, not the one you measure".
entries.details:
Numbers: before -- `bbox_error_bound(26)` with n=180 gives 0.0040 mm, and the 0.005 floor swallows it; the true error is **0.0214** mm. After -- `2 * 1.25 * (1 - cos(pi/24))` = **0.02139** mm, against a measured **0.02141** mm (difference -- float32 STL rounding).
Second bug, found while testing: the first fix put the term in `max(bbox, mink, floor)` -- and the part **still failed**, because `diff 0.0214 > tol 0.0214`. Cause: `max()` **drops** the float32 storage margin when the tessellation bound exceeds it. Errors **add**, they are not maxed. Final: `max(bbox_error_bound, floor) + mink`.
Why a separate term and not a bigger floor: raising the floor to 0.03 mm would also have loosened parts WITHOUT `minkowski()` -- and those were validated at 0.005 mm and catch real 0.45-1.4 mm mismatches. Now `mink = 0` for such parts and the tolerance is unchanged.
Checked that nothing loosened: `node` -- PASS with tol 0.0264; `post.stl` X -- still FAIL at 29.98 mm. New fixture `dimensions_minkowski_sphere_pass` + the old `dimensions_bbox_fail` -- both pass. Suite: **27 passed, 0 failed**.
Honesty: `minkowski_sphere_deficit()` resolves only what it can: `sphere(r = <number>)`, `sphere(r = <ident>/<number>)` and `sphere(r = <ident>)`. For an unresolvable radius the term is **skipped**, not guessed -- an invented radius would silently widen the tolerance, which is exactly what the whole module guards against.

entries.title: 8 checkers had not a single test; writing them I found a vacuous PASS
entries.symptom: Without tests were: `check_assumptions`, `check_dependencies`, `check_intake`, `check_plan`, `check_rules`, `check_service_envelope`, `doctor`, `scad_tessellation`. `scad_tessellation` was **just changed** today (minkowski term) and had not a single test.
entries.root_cause: `rules_manifest.yaml` R-04 had `applies: \"always\"` and `success_pattern: \"CHECK_RESULT connectivity=(PASS|SKIP)\"`. With no parts, `validate_scad.sh` correctly prints `connectivity=SKIP` -- but the SKIP was read as success. A rule that cannot be executed is **N/A**, not PASS.
entries.fix: new `applies` detector `glob_exists:<pattern>` -- `file_exists` cannot express "there is something to check". R-04 is now `glob_exists:parts/*.scad,assembly.scad` with `success_pattern: \"CHECK_RESULT connectivity=PASS\"` (no SKIP). Checked: empty project -- `R-04 N/A`; `rack_v4` -- `R-04 FAIL` (it really has separate bodies).
entries.promoted_to_rule: No -- proposed: "have a test for every checker; and a rule with no executable gate is N/A, never PASS".
entries.details:
Without tests were: `check_assumptions`, `check_dependencies`, `check_intake`, `check_plan`, `check_rules`, `check_service_envelope`, `doctor`, `scad_tessellation`. `scad_tessellation` was **just changed** today (minkowski term) and had not a single test.
Vacuous PASS, found while writing the `check_rules` fixture: `check_rules.py` in an empty project directory returned `exit 0` and printed `[PASS  ] R-04: Connectivity: every printed part renders as one connected body` -- for a project with not a single part.
Why this is worse than a FAIL: a FAIL says "failed". A vacuous PASS says "checked" about work that did not happen. Same class as the false PASS with a non-rendering part found this morning.
8 fixtures, all pass: the most valuable are not the happy paths but the contracts: `check_intake` returns **2** (no manifest) vs **3** (bad spec) -- the difference validate_scad.sh as caller wants; `check_rules` -- **3** (rule not met) vs **4** (checker run wrongly); `doctor` -- 0/2/3. `tessellation_minkowski_sphere` pins 0.021388 = 2*1.25*(1-cos(pi/24)), i.e. the real measured error, not an invented one.
Suite: 27 -> **35 passed, 0 failed**.

entries.title: SKIP without instructions: 8-10 checks do not run and nothing says what to do
entries.symptom: `attachment` was SKIP in **11/11** projects, `intake` 11/11, `bore_reachability` 10/11. The message only said what was missing ('no bores.json in project root'), not what to do.
entries.root_cause: the templates `templates/bores.json` and `templates/attachments.json` **did not exist at all** -- there was only `joints.json`. The checks were written and tested, but nobody could know how to prepare their input.
entries.fix: (1) both templates created and registered in `templates/README.md` with field explanations. (2) SKIP messages now name the concrete template and the consequence: `'SKIP: no bores.json -- copy templates/bores.json to the project root and fill it in; until then no bore is checked for reachability'`.
entries.promoted_to_rule: `server_rack_modular` -- '10 passed, 0 failed, 8 skipped'; `front_swerve_module` -- '8 passed, 0 failed, 10 skipped'. Suite: 35 passed, 0 failed.
entries.details:
And numbers in the output, not just in the log: the end of the run now prints `'COVERAGE: N passed, N failed, N skipped (N checks reported).'` and, if SKIP > 0, `'  N check(s) did NOT run -- each SKIP above names what it needs. A green run with a large SKIP count has verified less than it looks.'`.
Why it matters: `'All validations passed.'` and `'COVERAGE: 8 passed, 0 failed, 10 skipped'` are **different claims**, and now they are always printed together. Before, a green run could be read as a full check.
Technical detail: counted inside `log_check()` -- the only place every check passes through. The alternative was changing ~30 `echo` sites and collecting an array; a single choke point is both less code and cannot be skipped.
Already promoted to a rule?: No -- proposed: "a green run with a large SKIP count is not a full check; both numbers are printed together".

entries.title: SAKNIS: skill'o darbo eiga niekada neliepe parasyti deklaraciju
entries.symptom: `bores.json` and `attachments.json` existed in **0 of 11** projects. `attachment` SKIP 11/11, `bore_reachability` SKIP 10/11, together 95 SKIPs out of 198 check-runs.
entries.root_cause: the declarations are mentioned in SKILL.md **only in the checker table** -- as "what the check needs". No workflow step says "create this file". An agent reading carefully from §0 to §8 never learns they are needed.
entries.fix: §0.6 already requires exactly this knowledge in prose ('Insertion path', 'Shared-part neighbors', 'Retention', 'Purchased-part fit'). Added a table mapping each answer to its machine form: insertion path -> `bores.json`; neighbors -> `fusions.json` + `EXPECTED_BODIES`; retention -> `attachments.json`; purchased-part fit -> `joints.json`. No new step -- the same answers, written so that a check reads them.
entries.promoted_to_rule: No -- proposed: "if a check needs input, the workflow must require that input; otherwise the check exists only on paper".
entries.details:
And a contradiction in the skill's own text: §0.6 line 126 says §7 'closes two of the three with a real automated check (`check_bore_reachability.py`, `check_subfeature_overlap.py`)'. But those checks had no input -- so they **never ran on real work**. The claim was false from the day it was written.
Lesson: the 95 SKIPs were not a user problem and not a checker problem. It was a **workflow** problem: the checks needed input nobody asked for.
Not enough: adding the table is necessary, not sufficient. Need to check whether the agent follows it -- i.e. whether projects after this have the declarations.

entries.title: Degeneruota geometrija: 28 nanometru briauna sugadina spinduliu matavimus
entries.symptom: `check_printability.py` failed 4/4 real parts. Before tuning thresholds I checked whether its numbers can be true. On a clean model it is ACCURATE: solid 30 mm cube -> min 30.000 mm; hollow with exactly 3 mm walls -> min 3.000 mm.
entries.root_cause: `frame_module.stl` -- watertight, 1 connected body, all volume checks clean, and the shortest edge is 0.000028 mm (28 nanometres), 9 edges < 1 micron. On such a sliver the ray measurement reads a 0.014 mm wall -- 30x less than anything the model declares.
entries.fix: `check_connectivity.py` now reports DEGENERATE GEOMETRY with the shortest edge and the count, and says WHICH measurements it corrupts (printability wall/overhang) and that the slicer may get confused too. It is not a verdict -- the part is still one body, and PASS stays.
entries.promoted_to_rule: `connectivity_degenerate_edge_note` -- a tangent cylinder boolean with a 0.0005 mm offset gives a 250 nm edge. Checks three things: the note is there, it cites the edge, and a CLEAN mesh stays silent (otherwise the note becomes noise and stops being read). Suite: 35 -> 36 passed, 0 failed.
entries.details:
Control case: `base.stl` -- shortest edge 0.296 mm, measured wall 0.252 mm. They agree -- real geometry there, and `check_printability.py` is right.
Why not a new checker: this is a mesh integrity fact, and `check_connectivity.py` already splits components and already has the mesh in hand. A 17th checker would be one more file, one more SKIP and one more fixture for the same thing.
What this means for printability: it is not broken -- it is correct on a clean mesh and worthless on a corrupted one. While models have slivers, its thin-wall verdict cannot be a gate. Recorded in NEXT.md.
Already promoted to a rule?: No -- proposed: before trusting a ray measurement, check that the mesh has no sub-micron edges.

entries.title: check_subfeature_overlap was written, tested and NEVER run
entries.symptom: `subfeature_overlap` SKIP in **11/11** projects. `references/validation.md` made it 'manual, needs solo sub-feature STLs' -- i.e. admitted the check exists but nobody runs it.
entries.root_cause: the check needs SOLO sub-module STLs (each sub-feature separately, before `union()`). No project produces them, and **nothing in the skill produced them** -- there is no `MODE`/`PART` analogue for sub-features. Fed whole parts it reports meaningless overlaps (measured: 196 779 mm3 between two parts that only share a coordinate origin).
entries.fix: (1) `templates/part_template.scad` gets a `// SUBFEATURES: a, b, c` line, one module per name, and a **guarded** `SUBFEATURE` switch (same as the `assembly.scad` `MODE`/`PART` -- a plain assignment would destroy `-D`). (2) `validate_scad.sh` reads the line, renders each sub-feature SOLO and runs the check.
entries.promoted_to_rule: `// SUBFEATURES: tower_main, motor_cradle` with a deliberate overlap -> `'UNINTENDED SUB-FEATURE OVERLAP: demo__tower_main.stl <-> demo__motor_cradle.stl, 180.00 mm3'` and `CHECK_RESULT subfeature_overlap=FAIL`. Without the declaration -> SKIP **with a reason on stdout** (not only in the log), pointing to `templates/part_template.scad`.
entries.details:
Why this was costly: it is the only check that catches an overlap **inside one part**. A `union()` of two overlapping bodies is still one valid, watertight, single-body shell -- so `check_connectivity` and `dimensions` stay clean. Real incident (INCIDENTS.md 2026-08-19): the bearing tower overlapped the motor cradle by **419 mm3** inside one part and passed several "all green" rounds.
Separately PER PART, not globally: sub-features live in the part's LOCAL coordinates. Run as one set across several parts, two unrelated coordinate origins get compared -- exactly the false result I measured earlier.
New fixture: `subfeature_overlap_wired` -- runs `validate_scad.sh`, not the checker, because what was missing was the wiring, not the check. Checks both sides and that the line appears **exactly once** (found and removed a duplicate left over from the old "not a gate" block). Suite: 36 -> **37 passed, 0 failed**. The real project still has 18 checks.

Result: 10 findings, all confirmed by measurement: not one was a style remark.

F7 -- SKILL.md documented 0/2/3/4 for `validate_scad.sh`, which returns only 0/1: fixed.

F9 -- WORST: success on an unchecked project: `templates/README.md` sent files to `scad/`, while the gate globs `parts/*.scad` from the current directory. Result: 'no files found under parts/*.scad' -> **'All validations passed.', exit 0**, zero parts rendered. Fixed on both sides: README says 'project root', and an empty run now **fails** with an explanation and a pointer to `scad/parts/`.
F10 -- `templates/plan.md` said 'uncomment' the `PLAN_EXEMPT` line, while `check_plan.py` accepts only the `<!-- -->` form: fixed; checked that both forms behave as written.

entries.title: Silent false negative in my own tripwire: the inline parser fell into `|| echo 0`
entries.symptom: after the F1 fix (file size -> bounding box) I reran the 11 projects and noticed a **contradiction**: `collisions` now failed in 5 projects, and `server_rack_modular_v4` again showed **136 pairs with an identical 'penetration depth 170.000 mm'** -- the signature of 17 copies.
entries.root_cause: (1) the inline `python3 -c` assumed the STL is **binary** (4-byte triangle count at offset 80). OpenSCAD writes **ASCII** by default ('solid OpenSCAD_Model'), so the parser read ASCII as a number (943009847) and failed. (2) The call was wrapped in `2>/dev/null || echo 0` -- so the error turned into a **silent "nothing suspicious"**. The tripwire stopped detecting anything and nothing reported it.
entries.fix: separate `scripts/stl_extent.py` with a test. It reads BOTH formats (ASCII and binary), and on error **returns non-zero** and says what it could not read -- no `|| echo 0`. The gate now: if measuring fails, `collisions=SKIP` with a reason, not a guess.
entries.promoted_to_rule: renders ASCII, converts to binary via trimesh, and requires **both** to give 10x20x30; also a garbage file must return an error, not a number.
entries.details:
Why this is the same class I have been fixing all day: a silently swallowed error turned into success. Only this time -- in my own code, and exactly in the fix that removed a false positive.
Checked in both directions: `server_rack_modular_v4` -- **17/17 caught** (`'have exactly the assembly's bounding box'`); `examples/gear_reduction` -- `collisions=PASS`, `mechanics=PASS`, does not fire.
Learned: when removing a false positive, check that the new code still **catches the real case**. I did not do that right away -- I did it only because I reran all projects and noticed the numbers did not add up.
Suite: 40 -> **41 passed, 0 failed**.

entries.title: Five verdicts instead of two: printability was LABELLED SKIP even though it RAN
entries.symptom: an adversarial cross-disciplinary reviewer, asked to check whether other fields have already solved these problems.
entries.fix:
`PASS` / `FAIL` / `SKIP` (not applicable) / `INCONCLUSIVE` (ran, could not determine) / `ADVISORY` (ran, not a gate).
  - `printability` -> **ADVISORY** (it ran; FP share 4/4 = ~100 %, which is **above** the literature's >50 % "not worth integrating" threshold, so it reports but does not block)
  - the three `collisions` cases and `mechanics` without `assembly.scad` -> **INCONCLUSIVE**
  - `check_rules.py` -> new `[INCONC]` verdict; it is **not** `FAIL` (FAIL = fix the model, INCONC = fix the checker or its input) and the run stays non-green
  - COVERAGE line: `'COVERAGE: 6 passed, 3 failed, 7 not-applicable, 1 inconclusive, 1 advisory (18 checks reported).'`
entries.promoted_to_rule: `server_rack_modular_v4` -- `collisions=INCONCLUSIVE` (MODE broken), `mechanics=FAIL` (contract violation), `printability=ADVISORY`. Suite: **41 passed, 0 failed**.
entries.details:
What was wrong: `printability` ran on **4/4** real parts and found something in each. I labelled it `SKIP`, and SKIP means "not run / cannot determine". That is a **false claim about the tool** and it hides the finding from a future maintainer.
The standard I did not follow: `SKIP` merged three different things -- "not applicable", "ran but could not measure" and "ran but not a gate". They call for three different actions. SARIF `result.kind` separates `notApplicable` from `open`; TTCN-3 `verdicttype` has five values (`inconc` and `none` are verdicts, not annotations); pytest returns **6** for an empty run, not 0.
The cost of mislabelling: the Google Tricorder experience -- they **removed** user-level tuning, fixed root causes and **TURNED OFF** the HTML linter entirely. Their recorded lesson: suppression "caused hidden bugs".
Why INCONCLUSIVE must never become FAIL: that would merge a three-valued problem into two -- the same thing the reviewer had already found in the P2 decision. An inapplicable check reporting FAIL is a **false positive**.
What was left undone from the reviewer's list: (a) a pervasiveness rule -- which SKIPs contaminate the verdict (ISA 705); (b) a cover-property analogue -- whether each rule's antecedent ever fired (6 never did); (c) negative evidence -- whether a check can fail at all.

entries.title: Cover report, negative evidence and pervasiveness (carried over from the research)
entries.symptom: Three things I found only thanks to the research, and which had not been done
entries.promoted_to_rule: requires that COVER is present, that it **names** the rules (not just counts them), and that PERVASIVE appears, and if the run is green -- the OK line carries the number.
entries.details:
Three things I found only thanks to the research, and which had not been done
1. COVER report (analogue of the formal-verification "cover property"): in formal verification every `assert property` must have a paired `cover property` on its antecedent, and the cover **must be hit**: a passing assertion whose antecedent never fired is a **verification gap, not a success**. `check_rules.py` now prints `'COVER: 4 rule(s) exercised, 8 whose antecedent never fired: R-01, R-02, R-06, R-09, R-11, R-12, R-14, R-18'` and names them. Before, each run honestly said "N/A", but **the accumulation was invisible**: 6 of 18 rules had not fired in a single one of the 11 projects.
2. Negative evidence: on the formal side, an assertion that **cannot** fail is vacuous in a second way (`vacuous` tool classes: `constant-assertion`, `no-assertions`). The audit showed: **15 of 17 checkers have a fixture where they fail; 2 did not** -- `check_dependencies` (only a positive one: the change tree works) and `doctor` (only positive: reports on the machine). Both created: `dependencies_reaches_part` checks that a change **reaches** a part (C2, not C1) and names it; `doctor_reports_degraded` breaks a dependency via `PYTHONPATH` and requires `doctor` to **say so and name the consequence**, not return a clean bill of health.
3. Pervasiveness (ISA 705): the audit standard: when evidence cannot be obtained and the effect may be **material AND pervasive**, the auditor **disclaims an opinion** rather than giving a clean one. `check_rules.py` now: if more than half of the automated rules did not fire, it prints `PERVASIVE` and the OK line carries the number (`'only 4 of 12 automated rules had their antecedent fire'`).
I also found my own bug: the first version put the `PERVASIVE` block **after** `if any_auto_fail: return EXIT_FAIL`, so in a failing project it **never showed up** -- i.e. exactly where it matters most. Moved up.
Suite: 43 -> **44 passed, 0 failed**.
What is still left from the reviewer's list: mutation measurement of the golden set and re-measuring cost.

## Pattern analysis (Phase 2, 2026-08-19)

First real pass over the accumulated log (9 entries, 2026-08-16 to
2026-08-19) -- three recurring patterns, not just isolated incidents. For
each: the concrete mechanism Perplexity research turned up, honestly ranked
by precedent strength. **None of this is implemented yet** -- research and
write-up only, per explicit instruction; do not build from this section
without a separate go-ahead.

### Pattern 1 -- a declared/documented value drifts from what the live code
actually computes, after the live computation is upgraded

**Status (2026-08-22): implemented**, though as the "solo-scale guard"
variant described below, not the full shared-helper-function convention
-- see the 2026-08-22 entry in Entries for what was actually built and
tested (`scripts/check_margin_provenance.py`, R-15).

Instances: CD1/CD2 vs `gear_dist()` (below), `EXPECTED_BBOX` Z rounding
(below), `jackshaft_bearing_wall_at_diff` assert omitting real clearance
terms (below). Three of nine entries -- the strongest cluster in the log.

**Proposed mechanism** (moderate precedent -- fits "contract programming" /
dependency-integrity thinking, not a single named standard): stop writing
safety margins as separate handwritten numbers. Make the margin a function
that *calls the same helper function* the real geometry-cutting code calls
for its clearance terms, so there is no parallel arithmetic to drift apart
in the first place:

```scad
function shaft_clearance(d_nom, fit_class, printer_bias) =
    d_nom + fit_delta(fit_class) + printer_bias;
function shaft_safety_limit(...) =
    shaft_clearance(...) - safety_subtraction(...);
assert(shaft_safety_limit(...) > min_wall,
       str("shaft_safety_limit=", shaft_safety_limit(...)));
```

Solo-scale guard version (no full parser needed): a small script that scans
`.scad` files for `assert(`/`EXPECTED_*` and checks whether the formula it
references shares a helper-function name with the "live" formula used
elsewhere for the same quantity -- a lightweight dependency map, not full
static analysis.

### Pattern 2 -- a correctly-reasoned intentional contact (e.g. a clamshell
split line) never gets formalized into the declaration file meant to check
for exactly it

**Status (2026-08-22): implemented**, except the stability sub-check
(re-render with a jittered parameter to see if a verdict flips) --
explicitly out of scope, needs a real re-render per candidate pair. See
the 2026-08-22 entry in Entries (`check_collisions.py`
CANDIDATE INTENTIONAL TOUCH / NEAR MISS).

Instance: `check_collisions.py` failing on `gearbox_case_bottom`/`top`
(below) despite the touch being correctly identified as benign during the
original design session.

**Proposed mechanism** (most bespoke of the three -- no single standard
pattern, but aligned with BIM/CAD clash-tolerance practice): don't just
report "collision" -- classify the event (interference / contact / near
miss) and auto-suggest a declaration stub for human confirmation instead of
relying on someone remembering to write one by hand:
- overlap volume > 0 → real interference, flag as before.
- overlap volume == 0 and separation ≤ a touch tolerance (~0.02-0.05mm for
  printed parts) → candidate intentional touch, auto-generate a
  `joints.json` stub (part pair, `intentional_touch`, evidence, tolerance
  used) for the human/agent to confirm rather than hand-write from scratch.
- small positive gap below a separate, larger near-miss tolerance
  (~0.1-0.2mm) → flag as a near-miss, do NOT auto-declare (this is likely a
  real design sensitivity, not a benign touch).
- stability check: if a tiny parameter jitter flips the verdict between
  touch and overlap, treat it as a real problem, not benign -- don't
  auto-suggest in that case.

### Pattern 3 -- one shared params.scad variable is referenced by multiple
parts that each have a DIFFERENT real hard constraint, and only one
context's constraint gets checked

**Status (2026-08-22): implemented**, matching the proposed mechanism
closely (`use_param()` + a checker scanning for a matching assert() per
declared context). See the 2026-08-22 entry in Entries
(`scripts/check_param_context.py`, R-16). All three patterns from this
2026-08-19 pass are now implemented as of the same day.

Instance: `axle_d=6mm` shared across the diff-side stub (photo-measured,
~6mm) and the wheel_hub end (MR105 bearing, fixed 5mm ID) (below) -- only
the diff-side context was ever actually verified against.

**Proposed mechanism** (strongest precedent of the three -- directly maps to
established CAD constraint-dependency-graph research and to dependency
tracking in systems like PostgreSQL, which won't let you break an object
with unresolved dependents): a parameter provenance/context manifest. Each
part file that consumes a shared parameter for a hardware-fit purpose
declares which context and which constraint it's satisfying:

```scad
use_param("axle_d", "diff_stub_end", "photo_measured_~6mm");
use_param("axle_d", "wheel_hub_bearing_end", "press_fit_MR105_bore5mm");
```

A small checker scans for every parameter referenced by ≥2 `use_param()`
contexts and fails if any context's declared constraint was never actually
exercised by a matching `assert()` nearby -- catching exactly the failure
mode where one end of a shared dimension was checked and the other was
silently assumed compatible. Doesn't require a full requirements-
traceability system -- "no shared parameter may fan out into multiple hard
constraints without a manifest entry (and a real assert) for each fan-out."

### If/when this gets built

Perplexity's own suggested build order, if these get implemented later:
(1) the shared-helper-function convention for Pattern 1 (cheapest, closes
the strongest cluster), (2) the clash classifier + auto-suggest for Pattern
2, (3) the parameter context manifest for Pattern 3 (most novel tooling,
build last). Not scheduled -- logged here for when there's a go-ahead.

entries.title: golden set was too easy to measure anything (eval, N=10)
entries.where:
`golden_scad/golden_scad_10.json`, pre/post comparison of the
  RAG-hardening cycle (`golden_scad/PRES_PO_2026-09-11.md`).
entries.symptom:
the same 10 questions were run against the library BEFORE and AFTER
  a whole cycle of changes (passports, SKILL.md section split, retrieval.md, new
  rules, new checker). Both arms scored **100% on answer correctness**. The metric
  that was supposed to show improvement showed nothing.
entries.root_cause:
the questions were answerable from general OpenSCAD knowledge and
  a single obvious file. A discriminating eval needs cases where the "before"
  library genuinely cannot produce the right answer -- a question requiring the
  right one of two similar references, a chunk found by `applies_to` rather than
  by filename, or a trap where a plausible-but-wrong answer exists.
entries.fix:
before trusting a golden set, check it discriminates -- run both arms and
  confirm the score actually differs. If both are 100%, the set measures nothing.
  Needs ~30 cases and deliberately hard ones.
entries.promoted_to_rule: no -- this entry is the rule.
entries.details:
What DID move: source attribution (83% -> 100% evidence recall) and search
  cost (8.0 -> 3.8 files read per answer, -52%). So the cycle made answers cheaper
  and better-grounded, not more correct -- a real but different gain.
Also found: one case (SCAD-05) was not a valid control at all: the
  `openscad-organic` skill was untracked in git, so the `git worktree` "before"
  version lacked a file that existed on disk. The eval measured the worktree
  setup, not the library. And two rubric wordings of mine (Lithuanian diacritics:
  `kalibracij` vs `kalibravimas`) under-scored the "before" arm by 15pp until
  fixed -- an evaluator's own wording is a source of measurement error.

entries.title: motion_sweep.py gained a gear-ratio sign sanity check (Muse skill-analysis recommendation)
entries.symptom:
Motivation: an independent literature-and-skill-analysis research
  pass (`research_2026_scad_llm/`, using Muse Spark 1.3 Contributor to
  read the full `scad-modeler` `SKILL.md`) flagged that this script's own
  docstring had warned "getting the sign wrong is the easy mistake --
  meshing external gears turn opposite ways" since it was first written,
  but nothing ever actually checked it: a same-sign ratio on a declared
  `gear_mesh` pair produces a sweep that "passes" without the two gears'
  relative motion ever meaning what real meshing teeth would -- a
  misleadingly clean result on a mechanism that may not work at all.
entries.fix:
`check_gear_mesh_signs()` runs before any mesh is loaded or
  swept: for every declared `gear_mesh` contact whose both members are
  also drivers in the same `motion` block, requires opposite-sign,
  nonzero ratios. Deliberately scoped to `joint_type == "gear_mesh"` only
  -- a `worm_mesh`'s ratio relationship isn't a simple sign rule (large
  reduction across non-parallel axes), and a genuine internal/planetary
  mesh legitimately turns same-direction; declaring
  `"joint_type": "internal_gear_mesh"` opts a pair out of this check
  without disabling anything else about it.
entries.promoted_to_rule:
three fixtures added to the persisted regression suite --
  a same-sign reproduction of the real `pinion`/`spur` pair's shape
  (correctly fails, before any STL is even loaded, since fake STL paths
  were used deliberately to prove the check runs first); the same pair
  with the correct opposite signs (correctly passes the sign check,
  fails later only for the expected fake-STL reason); and an
  `internal_gear_mesh`-declared same-sign pair (correctly opts out).
  Full `validate_scad.sh --all` against the real `gear_reduction`
  example (whose `joints.json` already used the correct signs) stays a
  clean pass.

entries.title: added FDM printability checks (check_printability.py, R-17), grounded in an independent deep-research pass rather than a caught incident
entries.symptom:
Motivation: unlike every other entry in this log, not a caught bug
  -- a genuinely new capability, added after a deep-research pass was
  explicitly asked to find real, citable precedent (not just restate this
  project's own design) for pre-slicing FDM printability checks. The
  research graded its own findings honestly: overhang-angle and
  wall-thickness both "Strongest Precedent" (direct geometric techniques
  used in real tools -- face-normal-vs-build-axis for overhang, as
  Autodesk Meshmixer's "Overhangs" tool does; ray-casting for local wall
  thickness, a simpler alternative to full medial-axis-transform
  skeletonization); minimum feature size explicitly "No Strong Precedent
  Found" for a pre-slicing algorithm and NOT implemented as a result --
  most real tools defer that specific check to the slicer itself.
entries.fix:
`check_printability.py`, using only `trimesh` (already a
  dependency, via its ray-triangle intersector -- confirmed working
  without `pyembree` installed, using the pure-Python fallback). Two
  checks: (1) overhang -- flags downward-facing triangle area steeper
  than `--overhang-deg` (default 45) from vertical, EXCLUDING faces
  resting on the build plate itself (see bug below); (2) wall thickness
  -- samples up to `--wall-samples` face centroids, casts a ray inward
  along each face's own normal, flags any measured thickness below
  `--min-wall` (default 2x `--nozzle-d`, 0.8mm at the 0.4mm default).
  Standalone, not wired into `validate_scad.sh --all` -- new, not yet
  battle-tested at scale, and R-17 (manual) requires a human/agent read
  of the result rather than a bare pass/fail given the limitation below.
entries.promoted_to_rule:
a plain cube (clean pass after the baseplate-exclusion
  fix); a uniform 0.3mm-wall shell (correctly fails, measuring exactly
  0.300mm); a uniform 2mm-wall shell (correctly passes, measuring
  exactly 2.000mm, confirming no false positives at box corners); a
  gently-tapered cone at 33° from vertical (correctly does NOT flag
  overhang -- within the printable range, confirming the angle math
  isn't just "any downward slope fails"); a steeply-tapered cone at 77°
  from vertical (correctly DOES flag overhang, with the reported angle
  matching a hand calculation from the cone's actual dimensions exactly).
  Also run against the real `gear_reduction` example's `pinion.stl` and
  `spur.stl`: `spur.stl` passes clean; `pinion.stl` reports a borderline
  0.796mm minimum wall (just under the 0.8mm default threshold) at the
  small pinion's tooth root -- plausible, not obviously wrong, for an
  11-tooth module-1 gear, a known-marginal case for FDM in practice; not
  treated as a defect in the example, since this is a new, non-mandatory
  check and the example was never scoped against it.

Motivation: unlike every other entry in this log, not a caught bug
  -- a genuinely new capability, added after a deep-research pass was
  explicitly asked to find real, citable precedent (not just restate this
  project's own design) for pre-slicing FDM printability checks. The
  research graded its own findings honestly: overhang-angle and
  wall-thickness both "Strongest Precedent" (direct geometric techniques
  used in real tools -- face-normal-vs-build-axis for overhang, as
  Autodesk Meshmixer's "Overhangs" tool does; ray-casting for local wall
  thickness, a simpler alternative to full medial-axis-transform
  skeletonization); minimum feature size explicitly "No Strong Precedent
  Found" for a pre-slicing algorithm and NOT implemented as a result --
  most real tools defer that specific check to the slicer itself.
Bug found and fixed during testing (before this ever shipped): the
  first version flagged a plain 20mm cube's own flat BOTTOM face as an
  "unsupported overhang" -- its normal points straight down, which the
  naive check correctly measured as "facing down" but wrongly treated as
  floating, when it's actually resting directly on the build plate and
  needs no support by definition. Fixed by excluding any downward face
  whose height along the build axis is within `--baseplate-eps` (default
  0.05mm) of the mesh's own minimum height. Re-tested: the same cube now
  correctly reports zero overhang area.
Confirmed limitation (not fixed, documented instead): wall-thickness
  ray-casting can report a spuriously short distance near an EDGE where
  two non-parallel surfaces meet -- confirmed directly on a solid,
  non-hollow cone: its flat top cap measured a 0.13mm "thickness" near
  its rim, purely because the ray (cast along the cap's own straight-up/
  down normal) grazed the adjacent steeply-sloped side surface a short
  distance below, not because the part is actually thin there. Confirmed
  the technique IS reliable on genuine shell/enclosure geometry: a real
  2mm-wall box measured exactly 2.000mm with no artifacts at its own
  corners. Documented in the script's own docstring and both SKILL.md
  cross-references rather than engineering around it (would need a more
  sophisticated technique -- dual-direction ray averaging or true
  medial-axis analysis -- explicitly out of scope for this pass).
Already promoted to a rule?: Yes -- fixed directly in all listed
  files.

entries.title: added a parameter context manifest (use_param() + check_param_context.py, Phase-2 Pattern 3)
entries.symptom:
Motivation: third and final pattern from the 2026-08-19 pattern-
  analysis pass, implemented after the user asked for a "better skill"
  built from the accumulated cases. Real precedent: a single `axle_d`
  value fed both a diff-side output stub (photo-measured, fine at 6mm)
  and a wheel-hub bearing bore (fixed 5mm-ID MR105 bearing, incompatible
  with 6mm) -- only the diff-side context was ever actually verified
  against; nothing checked the wheel-hub context, and the incompatibility
  went unnoticed until someone traced both ends of the half-shaft by hand
  (INCIDENTS.md, 2026-08-18). This is the most novel of the three
  mechanisms (closest analogy: PostgreSQL refusing to drop an object with
  unresolved dependents), built last per the pattern write-up's own
  suggested order.
entries.fix:
`use_param(name, context, constraint)` is a no-op OpenSCAD
  module (defined once in params.scad, confirmed to compile and render
  cleanly as a statement with no children) that marks, at the point a
  shared parameter is consumed for a hardware-fit purpose, which context
  and which constraint it's satisfying. `check_param_context.py` scans
  every `.scad` file in the project for these declarations; for any
  parameter name declared in ≥2 distinct (file, context) pairs -- the
  only case with cross-context risk -- it requires the SAME FILE to also
  contain an `assert()` textually referencing that parameter name. A
  context with no matching assert() in its own file fails, naming exactly
  which context was never verified. Opt-in and a no-op when a project
  never declares `use_param()` at all. Wired into `validate_scad.sh`
  (auto, unconditional -- the script itself handles the nothing-to-check
  case) and `rules_manifest.yaml` as R-16.
entries.promoted_to_rule:
a direct synthetic reproduction of the axle_d incident
  shape (diff_stub.scad has its own assert, wheel_hub.scad declares the
  context but has none) correctly fails, naming the exact missing
  context; adding the missing assert to wheel_hub.scad correctly flips it
  to PASS; a single-context use_param() (no cross-context risk) correctly
  passes without requiring anything; a project with no use_param() calls
  at all (the real gear_reduction example) correctly passes as opt-in-skip.
  `use_param()` itself was rendered through real OpenSCAD twice --
  once inside a failing assert (confirmed the no-op module itself caused
  no parse/render error, only the assert on the following line failed, as
  intended) and once end-to-end with a passing assert (clean render,
  correct geometry, non-empty STL).

entries.fix:

  `--touch-tolerance` (default 0.05mm) is now classified CANDIDATE
  INTENTIONAL TOUCH -- still a FAIL (nothing auto-authorized), but printed
  with a ready-to-paste `joints.json` contact stub (pair names,

  requiring a human to replace it) instead of a bare "UNINTENDED

entries.title: added an analytic pre-flight gate, a provenance requirement, and a spatial "contact witness" to close the 12-round investigation class of defect
entries.symptom:
Motivation: a Perplexity deep-research pass (grounded in NASA/INCOSE
  V&V taxonomy, sequential-fault-diagnosis literature, and FreeCAD's
  dependency-DAG recompute model) was asked to optimize this skill's
  decision tree for fewer, cheaper validation rounds without sacrificing
  correctness. Its highest-priority finding: the single most expensive
  defect class found across every real project this skill has been used on
  (a 12-round investigation into a hidden collision, ending with a real
  `esp32_rc_modelis` incident where `big_gear`/`output_gear` radii summed to
  more than their actual center distance) was **purely algebraic** --
  discoverable from confirmed `params.scad` values alone, with zero need to
  ever render geometry.
- **Fix, three parts (all P0, "low cost / very high benefit" per the
  research's own priority ranking):**
  1. **Analytic pre-flight gate** in `validate_scad.sh`, running FIRST,
     before any part is rendered: every `assert()` in `params.scad` is
     evaluated via a trivial placeholder-solid wrapper (needed because a
     bare definitions-only file trips OpenSCAD's "empty top level object"
     hard-warning under `--hardwarnings` regardless of whether its asserts
     pass -- confirmed directly, and also confirmed that `assert()` failure
     alone does NOT change OpenSCAD's process exit code without
     `--hardwarnings` converting the resulting empty-object warning into a
     hard failure, a previously-unverified assumption this whole skill had
     relied on). Tested: a failing `r1+r2+clearance > center_distance`
     assert correctly fails with the real error message surfaced; a
     passing one correctly passes; no `params.scad` correctly skips; the

entries.title: edit classification (C1-C5) and forbidden_regions added (P2 decision-tree optimization)
entries.symptom:
Motivation: third-tier (P2) follow-up from the same 2026-08-21
  Perplexity research pass. P0 closed the validation side and P1 the
  change-propagation side of the 12-round defect class; P2 targets two
  smaller, still-justified gaps the research flagged as "moderate benefit,
  low-to-moderate cost": (a) `check_dependencies.py --change` told an agent
  WHICH declared requirements a change reaches (P1) but not HOW MUCH
  re-validation that minimally requires -- an agent still had to guess
  whether a part-local change needs the full `validate_scad.sh --all`; (b)
  `expected_bounds` (P0) is a positive allow-list (the contact must stay
  INSIDE one box) with no way to instead name a specific nearby feature
  that must NEVER be touched when the legitimate contact zone itself is
  awkward to bound tightly.
entries.fix:
1. **Edit classification (C1-C5)** in `check_dependencies.py`: a
     `classify_edit()` function maps the signals `--change` already computes
     (affected part basenames, affected declared contacts/motion/bores from
     the P1 cross-reference) to the cheapest class of re-validation actually
     needed -- C1 (nothing tracked reached) through C5 (reaches a declared
     motion driver -> full `validate_scad.sh --all`, since a motion/ratio
     change invalidates both the static collision precondition and the
     sweep). Advisory only, same fallback-to-full-`--all` discipline as
     every other advisory mechanism this skill has. Tested against all 5
     classes via synthetic fixtures, including one case where a variable fed
     a part that was ALSO a declared-contact member -- correctly returned
     C4 (contact) not C3 (bore), confirming the priority ordering
     (C5>C4>C3>C2>C1) matches the actual wiring rather than naive intent.
  2. **`forbidden_regions`** in `check_collisions.py`: the negative
     complement of `expected_bounds` -- a list of assembly-space boxes a
     declared contact must never touch, checked via AABB overlap against
     every detected contact region, failing as `CONTACT IN FORBIDDEN
     REGION` before the `expected_bounds` check runs. Tested with a
     synthetic two-bar fixture (one legitimate edge-clip contact, one
     illegitimate edge-clip contact inside a declared forbidden box): the
     illegitimate region is correctly caught and reported with its exact
     overlap location and volume; a second run with the illegitimate
     geometry removed (only the legitimate contact present) correctly
     passes with no false positive.

entries.title: added a validation-run log (scripts/validation_log.py) after a real reconstruction attempt lost almost all exit codes/commands/timestamps
entries.symptom:
Motivation: asked to reconstruct the steering_reduction_gearbox
  project's ~26-round validation history from `calculations.md` prose and
  this file alone (no live logging existed), the result had 24 of 26
  entries with an unknown exit code, unknown exact command, and unknown
  timestamp -- only the qualitative outcome (OK/FAIL + a described defect)
  survived. This is a real, demonstrated gap: `INCIDENTS.md`'s own stated
  purpose is "raw data for a later pattern-review pass," but the raw data
  was never actually being captured, only written up from memory
  afterward, lossily.
entries.fix:
`validation_log.py` is a small shared module (`log_run()` +
  CLI) that appends one JSON line -- timestamp, project dir, checker name,
  exit code, full command, short summary -- to
  `$SCAD_MODELER_LOG_DIR/validation_log.jsonl` (defaults to
  `~/.claude/scad_modeler/validation_log/` if that env var is unset;
  deliberately not a hardcoded personal path, since this script ships in a
  public repo). Wired into every `validate_scad.sh` `CHECK_RESULT` line
  and into the standalone entry point of every checker SKILL.md documents
  as commonly run directly (not just through `validate_scad.sh`).
  Best-effort: any logging failure is silently swallowed and never affects
  a check's own exit code. On this machine, `SCAD_MODELER_LOG_DIR` is set
  in `~/.zshrc` to `04_Kita/SCAD_Validacijos_Zurnalas/` (user's explicit

entries.title: added calibration_coupon() and a proactive-proposal rule (R-14) after the model only offered a fit-test print when explicitly asked, every time
entries.symptom:
in a separate
  real-project conversation (`20260821_serverrack`), the user had to
  personally ask, each time, for a part to be printed and checked for
  hole fit, and to be offered an incremental-diameter test rather than a
  single guessed dimension. `references/confidence-tiers.md` already
  names a calibration profile as a Tier 3 hard gate and
  `references/tolerances.md` already says "print a coupon ... and
  measure it" -- but nothing made the model actually PROPOSE that step
  on its own before finalizing a fit-critical dimension; the existing
  behavior was to silently note "uncalibrated, capped at Tier 2" rather
  than surface the concrete next action.
entries.root_cause:
the gap was between two already-correct pieces --
  `doctor.py`'s `find_calibration()` correctly detects a missing
  calibration profile, and `confidence-tiers.md` correctly says what
  that caps -- but no rule connected "profile missing" to "propose
  printing one," and no reusable coupon-generator existed, so proposing
  it meant hand-deriving hole-comb geometry from scratch each time (or,
  in practice, not proposing it at all until asked).
entries.fix:
`calibration_coupon(target_d, step, n_below, n_above, ...)` in
  `patterns.scad` generates a single labelled plate with through-holes at
  incremental diameters straddling a target size (using `true_hole_d()`,
  Pattern 0, so the coupon is built the same way a real part's holes
  are). `openscad-cad/SKILL.md` §4.5 now instructs proactively proposing
  a coupon print before finalizing a load-bearing/precision-sensitive fit
  with no calibration profile found -- not for every hole, only where
  being off actually matters. `scad-modeler/rules_manifest.yaml` R-14
  (kind: manual, since no script can verify a physical print happened)
  makes this an explicit self-assessment item in every §8 report for a
  project declaring `bores.json`/`joints.json`, cross-referenced from
  `scad-modeler/SKILL.md` §0.6's existing purchased-part-fit bullet.

  n_above=3)` rendered clean (manifold, non-empty, `--hardwarnings`

  incrementing 4.8/4.9/5.0/5.1/5.2/5.3mm, each legibly labelled;
  `check_rules.py` against the real `gear_reduction` example correctly
  lists R-14 among the manual rules requiring self-assessment.

entries.title: a BOSL2 gear positioned through layout.scad's at() failed under --hardwarnings; a plain guessed interference range was also wrong for real gear teeth
entries.where:
`scad-modeler/examples/gear_reduction/` (new example project,
  built for publication readiness -- see the "Publication prep" commits).
entries.symptom:
`validate_scad.sh --all` failed rendering `assembly.scad`
  with `WARNING: Ignoring unknown variable "$transform"` (from
  `BOSL2/transforms.scad`) and, after that was fixed, a second warning
  `"Ignoring unknown variable $parent_gear_pa"` (from `BOSL2/gears.scad`)
  -- both promoted to hard failures by `--hardwarnings`, which this
  skill's own `validate_scad.sh` deliberately uses.
entries.root_cause:
two distinct BOSL2 scoping gotchas, both real and neither
  previously hit by this skill's own testing because no earlier test
  fixture combined a BOSL2 module (`spur_gear()`) with the skill's own
  `at()` positioning pattern.
  1. BOSL2 redefines the built-in `translate()`/`rotate()` to also track a
     `$transform` special variable, used internally by `spur_gear()`'s
     attachable machinery. `layout.scad`'s `at()` module used the PLAIN
     built-in `translate()`/`rotate()` because `layout.scad` itself never
     included BOSL2 -- a module's `translate()`/`rotate()` binding is
     fixed at the scope where the module is *defined*, not where it's
     *called* from, so `parts/pinion.scad` including BOSL2 did not help.
  2. `BOSL2/gears.scad` declares `$parent_gear_pa` (and four sibling
     `$parent_gear_*` variables) as `undef` at its own top level, which is
     what normally makes reading them elsewhere not trigger "unknown
     variable". `BOSL2/std.scad` does NOT itself include `gears.scad`
     (confirmed by reading it directly). `parts/pinion.scad`'s own
     `include <BOSL2/gears.scad>` did not propagate to `assembly.scad`
     either, because `assembly.scad` only `use`s the part files, and
     `use` never propagates a file's top-level variable assignments (the
     same `use`-vs-`include` distinction already documented in
     `references/setup-notes.md`, hit again in a new combination).
entries.fix:
(1) `layout.scad` now includes `BOSL2/std.scad` then
  `BOSL2/gears.scad` itself, even though it never calls a gear function
  directly -- fixes both warnings, since a module's `translate`/`rotate`
  and special-variable visibility come from its own definition scope. (2)
  `joints.json`'s declared range widened to `[0.5, 2.0]mm` and
  `"multi_region_ok": true` added, both set from the actual measured
  values for this specific gear pair (documented inline in the file's
  `_comment`), not guessed. Full chain re-run after both fixes: `exit=0`,
  `check_rules.py` reports every applicable automated rule PASS.
entries.details:
Symptom (2), a real geometry finding, not a bug: once (1) was fixed,
  `check_collisions.py` correctly measured the declared `pinion`/`spur`
  gear-mesh contact at 1.383mm penetration depth, split into 2-3 disjoint
  regions -- both far outside a guessed `expected_interference_mm: [0.0,
  0.5]` range copied from earlier press-fit test fixtures, and enough
  disjoint regions to fail the new multi-region check without an
  exemption. Root cause: real involute gear teeth interpenetrate more
  deeply than a bearing/shaft press fit (module-1-scale addendum, not
  press-fit-scale), and a standard involute pair's contact ratio (>1 by
  design) means more than one tooth pair is legitimately in contact at
  once at any static pose -- this is normal, correct gear behavior, not a
  design defect.
